## Carrion decomposition and nutrient cycling in a semiarid shrub–steppe ecosystem

## ROBERT R. PARMENTER[1,3] AND JAMES A. MACMAHON[2]

> 1Valles Caldera National Preserve, P.O. Box 359, 18161 State Highway 4, Jemez Springs, New Mexico 87025 USA

> 2Department of Biology and the Ecology Center, Utah State University, Logan, Utah 84322 USA

Abstract. Vertebrate carrion decomposition and nutrient cycling have both direct and indirect effects on the soil properties, fauna, and flora associated with an animal’s carcass. While few comprehensive quantitative studies have been undertaken, those that have show considerable variability in decomposition processes and rates, their regulating variables, and the resultant ecosystem effects. In this two-part study, decomposition rates of vertebrate species were measured in a semiarid, shrub–steppe environment (Wyoming, USA). First, decomposition loss rates of mass, energy, and nutrients were measured for rat carcasses (Rattus norvegicus) in four seasons and two microsites (surface and underground burrows). Decomposition rates varied significantly between microsites (burrow . surface in spring and summer) and among seasons (spring . summer . autumn ’ winter), with mass loss amounts linearly correlated with ambient air temperatures. Energy and nutrient losses were related to phased carcass organ/tissue losses, with energy, K, Na, N, and S being lost more quickly than skeletal components (P, Mg, Ca). Overall, the nutrient loss sequence was K 1⁄4 Na . N 1⁄4 S . P 1⁄4 Mg . Ca. Carcass quality (N concentration) declined through time as a function of decay stage. Second, decomposition rates of 10 vertebrate species (mule deer [Odocoileus hemionus], dog [Canis familiaris], white-tailed jackrabbit [Lepus townsendii], Uinta ground squirrel [Spermophilus armatus], least chipmunk [Tamias minimus], deer mouse [Peromyscus maniculatus], Magpie [Pica hudsonia], Sage Sparrow [Amphispiza belli], terrestrial garter snake [Thamnophis elegans], and northern leopard frog [Lithobates pipiens]) were measured with vertebrate scavengers present or absent. Mass loss rates varied among species and were generally faster in the presence of scavengers. Carcass body mass, N content, or labile/recalcitrant fractions did not correlate with decomposition rate, though surface area to volume ratios of mammal carcasses were positively correlated with wet-mass decomposition rate. Nutrient measures of sub-carcass soils showed soil N, P, and Na increased during decomposition. Increased soil nutrient amounts represented up to 15.6% of the available carcass N, 28.8% of carcass P, and 28.7% of carcass Na. At a landscape scale in the shrub– steppe ecosystem, carrion decomposition constituted ,1% of the nutrient-cycling budget but contributed significantly to localized soil nutrient dynamics.

Key words: arthropod succession; ecosystem processes; Nicrophorus; nitrogen cycle; sagebrush–steppe; Wyoming, USA.

## INTRODUCTION

Decomposition and nutrient cycling of organic materials are critical processes that influence the structure and functioning of ecosystems worldwide. While considerable knowledge has been developed for the decomposition of plant litter materials (Lal et al. 1998, Stevenson and Cole 1999, Berg and McClaugherty 2003, Berg and Laskowski 2006), few studies have quantitatively addressed the decomposition processes of vertebrate carrion. The historic emphasis on plant litter decomposition can be attributed to the considerably larger quantities (and hence, ecosystem importance) of plant vs. animal biomass in most terrestrial ecosystems.

However, decomposing animal carrion can create localized islands of increased soil fertility, subsequently influencing local plant and soil invertebrate populations. While predators certainly capture and consume a large number of prey individuals, many animals die unseen by humans as a result of injuries, malnutrition, extreme weather conditions, parasites, and disease (Young 1994, Gulland 1995). Carrion as an energy and nutrient resource has driven the evolution of scavengers and decomposers (DeVault et al. 2003), and as will be discussed, has been shown to influence the structure, nutrient status, and faunal composition of sub-carcass soils, thereby contributing to spatiotemporal heterogeneity of adjacent plant assemblages. However, the ecological drivers and controls of the carrion decomposition process, while understood conceptually, have only begun to be detailed and quantified.

Qualitative understanding of the carrion decomposition process has been gleaned through many, some historic, observational time series studies (Me ́ gnin 1894, Motter 1898, Fuller 1934, Bornemissza 1957, Walker 1957, Reed 1958, Payne 1965, Coe 1978, Schoenly and Reid 1987) and numerous studies of arthropod successional patterns (e.g., Putman 1978a, Tantawi et al. 1996, Bourel et al. 1999, De Jong and Chadwick 1999, Koˇca ́ rek 2003, Watson and Carlton 2003, 2005, Tabor et al. 2004), particularly with respect to forensic entomology (Smith 1986, Byrd and Castner 2001, Gennard 2007). These and other studies have led to several qualitative classification schemes of decomposition stages, based on carcass condition and attendant arthropod species (see review by Carter et al. 2007).

Recent work has begun to quantitatively clarify the rates and limiting variables of carrion decomposition processes in some ecosystems, particularly with respect to carcass mass loss. Vertebrate carcass decay times, mass loss rates or decomposition coefficients (k values) have been reported for mice (Nabaglo 1973, Parmenter 2005), rats (Collins 1970, Putman 1978b, Koˇca ́ rek 2003), rabbits (De Jong and Chadwick 1999), coyotes (Scrivner 1985), pigs (Payne 1965, Hewadikaram and Goff 1991, Richards and Goff 1997, Davis and Goff 2000, Shahid et al. 2003, Grassberger and Frank 2004), elephants (Coe 1978), ducks (Parmenter and Lamarra 1991), salamanders (Regester and Whiles 2006), and several species of fish (Kitchell et al. 1975, Minshall et al. 1991, Parmenter and Lamarra 1991, Wipfli et al. 1998, Naiman et al. 2002, Stevenson and Childers 2004). Results from these studies, and those of human cadavers (Carter et al. 2007), have shown that vertebrate carrion exhibits substantially higher decomposition rates than plant materials, a finding consistent with the positive correlation between substrate quality (particularly nitrogen content) and decomposition coefficients (Swift et al. 1979, Cadisch and Giller 1997).

Studies of energy loss or nutrient cycling from vertebrate carcasses have identified nutrient loss sequences and rates in a limited number of aquatic and terrestrial systems (e.g., Kitchell et al. 1975, Putman 1978b, c, Parmenter and Lamarra 1991, Parmenter 2005, Regester and Whiles 2006). The influences of carrion decomposition on soil nutrient dynamics and/or adjacent vegetation have been documented in only four ecosystems: tallgrass prairie (Towne 2000), temperate forest (Melis et al. 2007), African scrub–savanna (Coe 1978), and arctic tundra (Danell et al. 2002). In addition, soil nutrient changes have been examined in the context of human cadaver decomposition (Vass et al. 1992). Nutrient mass transfer and secondary effects from large mammal carcasses and human cadavers in these studies showed significant influences on soil properties, resulting in localized changes in vegetation species composition, productivity, and nitrogen content. Bornemissza (1957) and Collins (1970) also documented changes in soil

faunal communities beneath decomposing rodent carcasses.

The purpose of this study was to quantify the decomposition processes of vertebrate carcasses in a semiarid, sagebrush–steppe ecosystem with respect to loss rates of carcass mass, energy, and nutrients, and to determine the influence of biotic and abiotic environmental factors in regulating the decomposition process. The experiments were designed to specifically test for differences in decomposition rates among seasons (spring, summer, autumn, winter), microsites (above- and belowground), carcass types (different species), and vertebrate scavenger activity (scavengers present or excluded). The experimental design allowed for quantitative analyses of nutrient changes in soils beneath decomposing carcasses over a three-year period.

In addition to evaluating these regulating variables on carrion decomposition processes, the results also could be applied to a comparison with known plant litter decomposition phenomena (see Berg and McClaugherty 2003, Berg and Laskowski 2006, and references therein). For example, plant litter decomposition generally exhibits faster rates below ground than above ground, and within similar microsites, decomposition rate is governed by moisture and temperature. High-quality litter (having greater N content) decomposes more quickly than low-quality litter, and plant litter quality (N concentration) increases through time, due to N enrichment from microbial processes; other nutrient concentrations during plant litter decomposition change in predictable patterns (e.g., Berg and Laskowski 2006:115). In some mesic ecosystems, larger pieces of litter (e.g., tree trunks) decompose disproportionately more slowly than small pieces (branches and twigs) as a function of surface area to volume ratios or stem diameters of the substrate (e.g., Foster and Lang 1982, Graham and Cromack 1982, Sollins 1982, Harmon 2001); however, in more xeric environments, the opposite is true due to more rapid loss of moisture in small diameter litter (Erickson et al. 1985). Given these documented phenomena of plant litter decomposition, to what degree do these decomposition patterns apply to vertebrate carrion decomposition?

Thus, the specific questions addressed in this study were as follows:

1) To what extent is decomposition rate (mass loss per unit time) correlated with seasonal changes in ambient temperatures?

2) Within seasons, are there differences in carrion decomposition rates below ground vs. above ground?

3) What is the composition of the carrion-associated arthropod assemblages in this shrub–steppe ecosystem, and how do these change through time and between microsites?

4) Are nutrient loss sequences and rates predictable from the nutrient composition of the animal’s organ/ tissue systems?

5) How does carcass quality (in terms of nutrient content) change as a function of time and decomposition stage?

6) To what degree do scavengers (considered to be ‘‘macro-decomposers’’) accelerate carrion mass loss in this ecosystem, and how does this change with seasons?

7) How do carcass mass-loss rates vary among wildlife species, based on body size, N-content, and morphological attributes (e.g., surface area to volume ratios, or skin type [scales, feathers, fur])?

8) To what degree do sub-carcass soils change in nutrient concentrations during carrion decomposition?

## Study site

The study site was located 8 km southwest of Kemmerer, Lincoln County, Wyoming, USA (41843[0] 30[00] N, 110838[0] 15[00] W, elevation 2255 m). Vegetation was classified as shrub–steppe (West 1983), dominated by big sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata Nutt.), little sagebrush (A. arbuscula Nutt.), antelope bitterbrush (Purshia tridentata (Pursh) DC.), Utah serviceberry (Amelanchier utahensis Koehne), and a variety of grasses (Poa spp., Achnatherum spp., Aristida spp., and Bromus spp.). Terrain was composed of rolling hills with a north–south strike, formed of Cretaceous limestones and sandstones; soils were loamy Ustifluvents. Climate is typical of high-elevation shrub–steppe, with annual precipitation averaging 248 mm, of which approximately half falls as snow during October through April (Appendix A). Annual snowfall (1948–2005) averaged 1.30 m/yr. Summer precipitation occurs in short-duration, high-intensity thunderstorms. Mean monthly temperatures are below 08C from November through March, and the summer growing season typically extends from early June to midSeptember.

## Seasonal and microsite effects on rat carcass decomposition

The first experimental objective was to quantify the influence on carrion decomposition of two abiotic variables: climate (season) and microsite. To distinguish these environmental effects, ‘‘standardized’’ small mammal carcasses were utilized in a replicated 4 3 2 factorial experimental design (four seasons 3 two microsites). Decomposition rates and nutrient loss dynamics were measured using carcasses of laboratory rats (Rattus norvegicus Berkenhaut) in four seasons (spring, summer, autumn, winter) and in two microhabitats (underground burrows and aboveground soil surface). Rat carcasses were obtained from the Utah State University animal rearing facility. Rats had been raised to a mean live body mass of 80 g (ranging from 74 to 90 g) and euthanized via cervical dislocation. Carcasses were then frozen at 208C until deployment in the field. (Note that freezing of vertebrate tissues results in intracellular damage and inhibition of internal bacteria that slightly biases the

decomposition process in favor of aerobic decay over anaerobic putrefaction during the first several days of decomposition [Micozzi 1986]. Frost damage to the skin also slightly increases the ability of arthropods [beetles and flies] to penetrate the carcass. In this study, this bias was assumed to be of minor extent, and all carcasses were frozen and treated identically prior to placement in the field.)

Three ‘‘control’’ rat carcasses were selected at random, weighed, and oven dried at 608C to constant mass to obtain a dry mass : wet mass ratio from which initial dry carcass mass values of the other rats could be estimated. Prior to deployment, carcasses were thawed and weighed to the nearest gram in the field using spring-loaded Pesola scales (Pesola AG, Baar, Switzerland).

Rat carcasses were placed in two microsites: surface and burrows. Surface carcasses were placed inside wire cages to prevent removal by vertebrate scavengers but allow access by carrion-feeding arthropods. Surface cages (n 1⁄4 45) were constructed of 12.7-mm mesh hardware cloth, with dimensions of 25 3 25 3 20 cm (L 3 W 3 H), and secured in place with two steel rebar stakes. Cages were set into the soil to a depth of 1 cm, to allow each rat carcass (one rat/cage) to lie in full contact with the soil surface.

Artificial ‘‘rodent burrows’’ (n 1⁄4 45) were created using a hardware cloth tube (60 cm long 3 5 cm diameter) dug into the ground at a 458 angle to a depth of ;40–45 cm. Paper towels were placed over the top of each tube prior to burial to prevent soil from filling the tube during installation. Rat carcasses (one rat/burrow) were placed at the bottom of the burrows, and the entrance to each burrow was wired closed with hardware cloth (again, allowing access by arthropods but not vertebrates). The burrow tube was then secured in place with a steel rebar stake.

Rat carcasses were placed simultaneously in cages and burrows during four seasons: spring (12 May, n 1⁄4 90 carcasses), summer (29 July, n 1⁄4 90), autumn (16 September, n 1⁄4 75), and winter (20 December, n 1⁄4 18). Replicate carcasses (n 1⁄4 3 carcasses/date) were collected at predetermined time intervals following each season’s initial placements; collection-time intervals varied somewhat by season, but samples were taken at day 79 in all seasons as a representative date for the end of that season. At the time of collection, carcasses were first inspected for attendant arthropods, and if present, representative voucher arthropod specimens were collected and later identified in the Insect Museum of the Utah State University Department of Biology (Logan, Utah, USA). Carcasses were then weighed in the field (wet mass), placed in individual plastic bags, transported to the laboratory, cleaned of attached soil particles and any remaining arthropods, and oven-dried to constant mass at 608C to determine remaining carcass mass. Dried carcasses were then ground in a Wiley mill to a fine powder for nutrient and energetic content analyses.

USA. Total nitrogen (N) was measured using the Kjeldahl method, while other mineral and salt concentrations (calcium, Ca; phosphorus, P; magnesium, Mg; sulfur, S; sodium, Na; and potassium, K) were measured with an inductively coupled argon plasma (ICAP) instrument using standard digestions and analytical procedures. Energy content (kJ/g dry mass) was measured in the Range Science Nutritional Analysis Laboratory at Colorado State University, Fort Collins, Colorado, USA, with an adiabatic oxygen bomb calorimeter.

Decomposition rates were estimated using dry-mass values from field-collected carcasses. These values were converted to percentage dry-mass remaining (PMR), based on the initial estimated dry mass of each carcass (using the dry-mass : wet-mass ratio developed from the ‘‘control’’ rat carcasses). Percentage dry-mass loss rates during each season in each microsite were calculated using the double-negative exponential model (Wieder and Lang 1982):

where PMR is the percentage mass remaining (%), A is a mass composition proportion, k values are decomposition constants (relative mass loss per day), and t is time (days). This model recognizes two component fractions of materials comprising the rat carcass, with each having a different decomposition rate (k value): a labile fraction (A) made up of easily decomposable materials (muscle and other soft tissues) characterized by a high decomposition rate (k1) and a remaining recalcitrant fraction (1  A) made up of bones, hide, and hair and characterized by a much slower decomposition rate (k2). The sum of these two terms (Ae[][k][1][t] and (1  A)e[][k][2][t] ) represents the total percentage remaining mass of the carcass at time t.

Statistical tests for differences in PMR between microsites and among seasons were conducted using analysis of variance (ANOVA) with a completely randomized factorial design (two microsites and four seasons) with two-way interactions (Wieder and Lang 1982). Individual rats were treated as the experimental units (replicates). Least-significant difference (LSD) analyses of the means for PMR were used to identify specific instances of significant differences among microsites or seasons. Nutrient loss sequences were determined through ANOVA of the mean percentage of each nutrient remaining as a function of rat carcass PMR; in addition, an analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) was conducted to test for differences in the slopes of nutrient losses from rat carcasses with changes in rat PMR. Finally, changes in concentrations of nutrients in rat carcasses in different stages of decomposition, and through time, were characterized with linear and nonlinear regression analyses. Model selections of linear, exponential, logarithmic, polynomial, or power equations were conducted using maximal correlation coefficient values. Statistical significance for all analyses was defined as P  0.05.

## Carcass-type effects and scavenger impacts

The second experimental objective was to compare decomposition rates among representative native wildlife species and to determine the effects of vertebrate scavengers (e.g., coyotes, vultures, Magpies) in accelerating the decomposition process. To test for differences in carrion decomposition rates among wildlife species, carcasses were obtained for six species of mammals, two bird species, one snake species, and one frog species (Table 1; hereafter, these species will be referred to in the text as mule deer, dog, jackrabbit, ground squirrel, chipmunk, deer mouse, Magpie, sparrow, snake, and frog). These species represented a body mass range of greater than three orders of magnitude. Based on this experiment, decomposition rates were expected to be faster in small-bodied species (with greater surface area to volume ratios) than large-bodied species. In addition,

these species presented a range of carcass nitrogen values, allowing for a test of N content as a correlated factor with soft-tissue decomposition rate (k1 values). This species list also provided material with which to evaluate wet- and dry-mass losses from carcasses with different skin covering: fur on mammals, feathers on birds, scales on snakes, and water-permeable skin on amphibians. Wet- and dry-mass loss rates were predicted to be faster in species with water-permeable skins vs. water-impermeable skins (e.g., frog . snake; Goin and Goin 1971, Duellman and Trueb 1986).

All wildlife species were resident in the area (Parmenter et al. 1985), except for dogs, which were used as a substitute for the dominant native canid, the coyote (Canis latrans Say). Specimens of most species were road-killed individuals, collected fresh (within 12 h) from highways; exceptions included dog carcasses (obtained from the Logan, Utah, USA, city dog pound following euthanization by the city veterinarian), frogs (leftover from university instructional laboratories), and deer mice and chipmunks (collected during other research studies). Specimens (n 1⁄4 6 per species) were frozen shortly after collection in a walk-in freezer at 208C until field deployment. Care was taken in selecting fresh roadkilled wildlife carcasses to ensure that the skin was not perforated (which could have altered arthropod access and microbial putrefaction processes) and that the carcass had not lost substantial quantities of blood (which may have altered the moisture and nutrient status of the carcass). Additional ‘‘control’’ specimens (except mule deer and dogs) were collected for initial nutrient and energy content analyses (Table 1); initial values for mule deer and dogs were obtained from literature sources or estimated from other mammal species.

It should be noted that, unlike the rat experiment in which all specimens had been raised in captivity and were similar in body size, mass, and nutritional condition, the wildlife specimens were more variable in carcass characteristics. While all were generally adult animals, differences in body size and mass indicated a variety of age classes. It has long been known that nutrient content in an animal’s body changes with age and development (e.g., Spray and Widdowson 1950), and this phenomenon, along with potential differences in health and nutritional status among the specimens of each species at the time of death, may have influenced the overall nutrient content of the experimental population of carcasses, thereby contributing to the inherent variation in the decomposition processes.

Carcasses were thawed and placed in the field in summer (1 July) in one of two randomly assigned treatments (n 1⁄4 3 replicates/treatment): open surface (accessible by vertebrate scavengers) and caged (inside scavenger exclosures). Exclosure cages were constructed of wooden frames and 32-mm mesh poultry wire (Appendix B). A square piece of hardware cloth (12.7 mm mesh) was placed beneath each carcass to facilitate lifting of the carcass for weighing. Carcasses were

weighed in the field at predetermined time intervals for the first 15 months, at which time one carcass of each species from each treatment was collected and processed in the same fashion as the rat carcasses. Dried carcasses were analyzed for energy content and nutrients as described. The other carcasses remained in the field, were weighed at additional time intervals, and collected and processed similarly in the autumn (September) of years 2 and 3.

Decomposition rates were calculated for both dry- and wet-mass measurements using the doubleexponential model described above. Statistical tests of species and scavenger treatment differences in wet percentage mass remaining (PMR) were performed using repeated measures analysis of variance (RMANOVA) and LSD means comparison tests. Regression analyses (linear and nonlinear) were used to assess the relationships between decomposition rates (k1 values) or carcass PMR (as dependent variables) and initial carcass wet and dry mass, N content, proportions of labile/recalcitrant carcass tissues, and (for mammals and birds only) surface area to volume ratios (as independent variables).

Carcass locations were periodically inspected and the numbers of remaining carcasses were recorded.

## Carcass decomposition effects on soil nutrients

The third major objective of the study was to determine the degree to which carrion decomposition

altered the nutrient status of the soil beneath and adjacent to the carcass. Changes in soil nutrient concentrations associated with carrion decomposition were quantified during the wildlife carcass study. Plastic containers filled with soil were placed beneath each carcass (Appendix B) at the outset of the experiment. Container sizes varied depending on carcass type: deer carcass containers were circular (122 cm diameter 3 46 cm depth); dog carcass containers were somewhat smaller (91 cm diameter 3 38 cm depth); jackrabbit containers were rectangular (33 cm length 3 28 cm width 3 18 cm depth); ground squirrel and Magpie containers were 26 cm diameter 3 21 cm depth; and chipmunk, deer mouse, sparrow, snake, and frog containers were 10 cm diameter 3 15 cm depth. The containers did not have drain holes, to prevent leaching of materials out of the containers, and the container walls extended 2–3 cm above the soil surface to prevent gains or losses of materials through surface flow of water (snowmelt or thunderstorm precipitation). Soil for the containers had been collected locally, screened through a 1-mm sieve to remove gravel, pebbles, and coarse organic matter (twigs and so on), and thoroughly homogenized prior to filling the containers; these actions were necessary to provide a consistent, uniform soil substrate beneath all the experimental carcasses to assess nutrient changes through time. Control soil containers (26 cm diameter 3 21 cm depth, without carcasses; n 1⁄4 2) were used to monitor natural changes in soil nutrients over the three years of the experiment.

Soils were collected during carcass collections at 15-, 27-, and 39-month time periods. Soil tubs were emptied into large plastic bags in the field, and each entire container sample was oven-dried at 608C to constant mass and weighed to the nearest gram. The soil from each container was then thoroughly homogenized, and two replicate soil samples were analyzed from each carcass container. Soils were analyzed for N, P, K, Na, S, Mg, and Ca as described for the carcasses. Control soils were analyzed at time 0 and at 39 months.

Total amounts of each nutrient present in the subcarcass containers were calculated by multiplying the total dry mass of the soil from each container by the nutrient’s concentration. Increases in each soil nutrient’s amount were then compared to the available pool of that nutrient in the carcass. Statistical tests for temporal increases of each nutrient in the soil were conducted using ANOVA and LSD procedures as already described.

## Seasonal and microsite effects on rat carcass decomposition

Arthropod patterns.—In general, rat carcasses followed the typical pattern of carrion decomposition (e.g., Payne 1965), with an initial fresh stage of arthropod colonization, carcass bloating, and putrefaction from gasses produced by internal microbial processes, followed by an active decay stage with maximum arthro-

pod activity, then a drying phase, and finishing with a skeletal remains stage. Initial arthropod colonizations of the carcasses involved ants (Formicidae: Formica obscuripes Forel) and burying beetles (Silphidae: Nicrophorus guttulus Motschulsky, N. marginatus Fabricius, N. hybidus Hatch and Angell; Fig. 1). Burying beetles were common on rat carcasses in both surface and burrow microsites during spring and summer, successfully rearing young in the burrow microsites (the surface cages prevented burial of surface rat carcasses, but some Nicrophorus larvae were observed). Dermestid beetles (Dermestes fasciatus LeConte) were common on surface rat carcasses within a week of deployment in spring and summer, but absent from autumn carcasses. Larvae of flesh flies (Sarcophagidae) and blow flies (Calliphoridae) appeared on the carcasses at varying times following carcass deployment, depending on microsite and season (Fig. 1); warmer temperatures in summer were associated with shorter time intervals of fly larval activity in surface rat carcasses compared to spring and autumn, but belowground summer fly larval activity extended over longer periods than in any other season (Fig. 1). Fly larvae were observed throughout the winter in burrow carcasses that had been deployed in autumn, indicating that fly larvae could overwinter underground on rat carcasses. No other arthropods were observed on the autumn-deployed carcasses in winter, and no arthropods were observed on winter-deployed carcasses until the following spring. Fungal hyphae growths were common on burrow carcasses in autumn, and on both surface and burrow carcasses during winter when deep snow covered the study area from early November to late April.

Nutrient cycling patterns.—As noted above, rat carcass decomposition was primarily undertaken by arthropods during spring, summer, and autumn periods, with physical and chemical processes of secondary importance. Fly and beetle larvae consumed the highenergy and nutrient-rich portions of the carcass,

promoting the rapid mass loss of the carcass’s mobile fraction, while dermestid beetles slowly worked on the dried tissues and skin. Skeletal and pelage fractions exhibited little decay during the experiments. These tissues were composed of different chemical constituents, and as such, their loss rates and sequences from the carcass were associated with the feeding activities of the arthropods.

The soft tissues consumed by fly and beetle larvae were high in nitrogen (protein) and energy, and therefore these components were lost at a disproportionately high rate from the carcass compared to total mass loss during decomposition (Fig. 4). Water-soluble salts (Na and K) generally occur in bodily fluids, and could be consumed by arthropods, leaked out of the carcass, and/or leached out by rainfall or melting snow. These constituents were lost from the carcasses at a faster rate than N (Figs. 5, 6). Sulfur is found in proteins and throughout other soft tissues, and thus was lost at a rate similar to that of N. Skeletal components (Ca, Mg, and P) were lost very slowly from the carcasses (Figs. 5, 6), and comprised a major component of the remaining carcass in the later stages of decay. Some P was lost early in the process, presumably due to its presence as ATP, ADP, phospholipids, and nucleic acids in soft tissues and organs. ANOVA and ANCOVA results showed that the sequence of nutrient losses from rat carcasses could be summarized as K 1⁄4 Na . N 1⁄4 S . P 1⁄4 Mg . Ca (Fig. 6).

## Carcass decomposition effects on soil nutrients

Nutrient loss patterns in the wildlife carcasses mirrored those of the rat experiment, with K and Na being lost at the fastest rate, followed by N and S, and finally P, Mg, and Ca (Table 4). The soils analyses revealed significant increases in soil N under carcasses of mule deer, dog, jackrabbit, ground squirrel, sparrow, and frog (Table 5). Other nutrients that showed occasional increases in soil concentrations included K, S, Na, Mg, and P (Table 5, Appendix E), although patterns among species were not consistent. Calcium concentrations exhibited large fluctuations through time, even in control soil bins, potentially due to

depositions of wind-blown calcium-rich loess derived from nearby limestone outcrops.

Calculations were made of total mass amounts of each nutrient in the carcass at time 0 (Table 1) relative to the observed increase in mass of those nutrients in the soil bins (Table 5). After 15 months, soil nutrient increases represented up to 14.2% of the carcasses’ original N content, 22.7% of carcass Na, and 18.3% of carcass P. Soil enrichment persisted for some carcass types through the entire 39 months of the study. Calculations for soil amounts of K, S, Mg, and Ca for all species were .100% of original carcass nutrient mass, indicating that these soil elements had increased, at least partially as a result of allochthonous inputs; potential sources of these inputs were loess, arthropod carcasses, and frass (Frost and Hunter 2007), or urine/feces of scavengers visiting the carcasses (Bullard 1982).

## Carcass decomposition rates and temperature effects

The range of decomposition rates for the carcass labile fraction measured in this study was generally consistent with previous rate values measured for other vertebrate species in terrestrial ecosystems, although considerable variability was observed. Dry-mass decay constants (k1 values) ranged over two orders of magnitude, from 0.0016 to 0.1669 (Fig. 2, Appendix D), depending on species, season, and microsite location. Wet-mass decay constants observed in this study were predictably greater than dry-mass values as a result of rapid water loss from the carcasses in this semiarid environment. Across all 10 species examined, wet-mass decay constants ranged from 0.0553 to 0.7874 (Table 2). Mass loss rates of rat carcasses among seasons proved to be linearly related to mean daily ambient air temperatures. The temperature coefficients (Q10 values, Fig. 3) for both aboveground and belowground carcasses were very close to 2.0, indicating a doubling of decomposition rate for every 108C increase in temperature. While not quantified in terms of decay constants, previous observations on the decomposition of small- to large-bodied mammal carcasses in other ecosystems indicate that decomposition in warm, moist environments proceeds much faster than in extreme cold desert environments. Knott (1998) reported that an adult orangutan carcass in Borneo’s tropical forest was reduced to bones and hair in two weeks, whereas in the dry valleys of Antarctica, Pe ́ we ́ et al. (1959) observed well-preserved, ‘‘freeze-dried’’ carcasses of crab-eater seals that, when dated using radiocarbon analyses, were found to be 1600–2600 years old. Cornaby (1974) observed that reduction of toad and lizard carcasses to skeletal remains took only 6–7 days in a mesic environment in Costa Rica, but in the xeric site, carcasses desiccated and remained either partially or entirely intact. Similarly, human corpses in hot desert environments desiccate quickly, delaying the skeletal remains stage by up to six months (Galloway et al. 1989). In contrast, though, human corpses in subfreezing winter temperatures in Alberta, Canada, still decomposed to skeletal remains in as little as four weeks,

often associated with vertebrate scavenger activity (Komar 1998). In our Wyoming study site, carrion decomposition displayed a range of dynamics, with faster mass loss rates during warm, moist periods (spring and early summer) and slower rates during hot, dry summer conditions or subzero winter temperatures.

## Microsite effects on carcass decomposition rates

Decomposition rates also differed as a function of carcass location with respect to aboveground vs. belowground location (Fig. 2). Belowground rodent ‘‘burrow’’ environments in arid and semiarid ecosystems are typically cooler and more humid than surface environments (Degen 1997), providing ameliorated microclimate conditions for arthropod activities and microbial processes. As such, belowground carrion desiccation is slowed, allowing for more rapid and complete decomposition of the carcass in this semiarid shrub–steppe ecosystem. Similar results of microsite influences were obtained for rodent decomposition in forested and open sites in the Pacific Northwest, with belowground rodent carcasses consistently decomposing more quickly than surface carcasses in the same locations (Parmenter 2005). The results of our study also are consistent with other experiments investigating microsite effects on carrion decomposition. Wilson et al. Koˇca ́ rek (2003) found that rat carcasses decomposed more quickly in open meadow habitats compared to forested sites in the Czech Republic, due to associated warmer temperatures in the meadow environment. Similar patterns were observed by Sharanowski et al. (2008) and Shean et al. (1993) for pig carcasses placed in sunlit and shaded microsites. For example, rodent carcass decomposition rates measured across a disturbance gradient from old-growth forest to an open volcanic pumice plain on the Mount St. Helens volcano in Washington (USA) were fastest in the cool, damp forest and slowest on the hot, dry plain (Parmenter 2005).

## Carcass size, quality, and species effects on decomposition rates

Carcass size (mass), nutritional quality (N content), surface area to volume ratios, and taxonomic differences in epidermal water permeability were predicted to have substantial influence on decomposition rates. Carcass mass has been observed to influence mass loss rates due to larger carcasses having higher initial internal temperatures (promoting microbial decomposition and arthropod activity; Hewadikaram and Goff 1991). However, initial carcass mass was not correlated with either decay constants (k1) or mass loss amounts at any time period

It was apparent that larger carcasses supported vastly larger populations of fly and beetle larvae than smaller carcasses, and these greater numbers of arthropods were successful in reducing mass in the larger carcasses at proportionally the same rate as in small carcasses. This relationship held up both among and within major taxa (amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals).

Nitrogen content also was hypothesized to be positively correlated with decay rate, as N concentrations would be related to protein content and potentially greater amounts of soft tissues (labile fractions, A). However, no significant relationship was observed, presumably due to the similarities in N content found among the wildlife species in the experiments (Table 1) and the great speed with which arthropods removed labile tissues from the carcasses. Vertebrate carrion comprises a nitrogen-enriched resource, and arthropod population numbers quickly consumed these tissues regardless of differing N-content values across the range of species.

Carcass surface area to volume ratios of mammals were positively correlated to wet-mass k1 values and to wet-mass PMR during the first five days of decomposition. This relationship demonstrates that, for mammal

carcasses in arid and semiarid ecosystems, water mass loss can be predicted based on surface area to volume ratios. Water in xeric environments can be the limiting factor in decomposition processes, and small-bodied species with high surface area to volume ratios may desiccate before carrion-feeding arthropods, bacteria, and fungi can remove the labile fraction of the carcass. Even in large-bodied species, surface area to volume ratios have an influence on wet-mass loss rates. For example, Hewadikaram and Goff (1991) tracked wetmass PMR from two pig carcasses of different sizes (8.4 and 15.1 kg), and found faster mass losses of the smaller carcass (with a greater surface area to volume ratio) during days 1–5, but after that time (days 5–15), the larger carcass decomposed more quickly due to the presence of much larger carrion-feeding arthropod populations and warmer carcass temperatures.

The other carcass characteristic that exhibited a predicted outcome was the rapid desiccation of the frog carcasses, producing the most rapid wet-mass loss rate of the 10 species examined (wet-mass k1 1⁄4 0.787; Table 2). ## Nutrient-loss patterns during carcass decomposition

The carcass energy and nutrient-loss rates and sequences observed in this study appeared consistent with those of previous work. Water-soluble salts (K and Na) were lost first and most rapidly, most likely through leaching of body fluids into the soil and consumption of soft tissues by insect scavengers. Losses of energy, N, and S were closely associated with overall soft tissue consumption by invertebrate and vertebrate scavengers, as energy content and these nutrients are most commonly associated with muscle and body organs. Phosphorus is a component of both bones and soft tissues and was lost from the carcass at somewhat slower rates than N and S. Finally, Ca and Mg, most commonly found in skeletal materials, were the slowest nutrient to leave the carcass.

Similar patterns have been documented in the decomposition of rodents (Parmenter 2005) and fish and ducks (Parmenter and Lamarra 1991). Regester and Whiles (2006) observed rapid loss of N and C during decomposition of salamander carcasses and egg masses, but other nutrients were not assessed. Finally, Putman (1978b, c) quantified loss rates of C (as CO2) and energy from rodent carcasses, and found seasonal (temperature) differences associated with both microbial and scavenging insect activities.

The nutrient quality of carrion during decomposition exhibits considerable change as microbes and arthropods selectively remove the soft-tissue labile fraction of the animal’s carcass. As these protein- and carbohydrate-rich tissues are consumed, nitrogen, sulfur, and energy content values decline as a function of carcass PMR (Figs. 7, 8), as well as time (Figs. 9, 10). Belowground carcasses lose these components more rapidly than aboveground carcasses. Water-soluble salts (K and Na) also show rapid decreases in concentration with decay stage (Fig. 7), and steep exponential declines with time (Fig. 9). As predicted, recalcitrant skeletal constituents (P, Mg, and Ca) exhibit increases in concentration with both carcass condition (Fig. 8) and time (Fig. 10). This latter pattern does not appear to be the result of ‘‘enrichment’’ of the carcass from allochthonous sources, but rather a function of subtraction of other carcass tissues. ## Carcass decomposition effects on soils

Nutrient changes in the soils beneath vertebrate carcasses were observed in our study, although total mass transfers were relatively small. Total N increased in sub-carcass soils in the first and second years, representing up to 15.6% of the total N available in the carcasses. The source of this soil N is likely from the carcass itself, arriving through direct leaching of proteinrich fluids and small particles of body parts, as well as indirect transfer of N from carcass to soil via insect frass, exoskeletons, and pupal cases. However, it should be noted that the increased N may hypothetically occur from non-carcass sources, such as a possible increase in

N-fixing soil bacteria beneath the carcass. Further studies using, for example, 15N-enriched carcasses (similar to Frost and Hunter 2006) could elucidate these pathways and mass transfers of N.

Regardless of the source, carrion-decomposition processes in our semiarid study site appear to enrich the soils in the vicinity of the carcass, leading to changes in the localized plant community. Large mammal carcasses (e.g., see Appendix C for photograph of a mule deer carcass and adjacent vegetation) alter the microenvironment in terms of soil temperature, moisture, nutrient concentration, and physical structure. This produces a ‘‘halo’’ effect for neighboring plants, whose roots can reach the altered soils beneath and adjacent to the carcass. The carcass itself also acts to increase precipitation to adjacent soils via runoff from the

carcass; this water harvest would amplify the nutrient enhancement effects in the vicinity of the carcass. In this semiarid ecosystem, it may be that water from the decomposing carcass, coupled with precipitation runoff, may play an important role in nearby plant growth in addition to nutrient increases. For example, an adult mule deer contains ;50 kg of water (50 L), and depending on the proportion that infiltrates into the soil beneath the carcass, this amount could be equivalent to several storm precipitation events. Adjacent plants would certainly respond to such water enhancements in arid and semiarid ecosystems.

The role of carrion decomposition on soil nutrient status and nearby plant populations has been quantified in several studies. Collins (1970) noted that herbaceous plants within 20 cm of decomposing rat carcasses in a temperate oak forest grew taller and more dense for at least 18 months post-decomposition, suggesting a combination of soil-enhancing effects from potential carcass leachates and soil disturbance by carrionassociated insects (e.g., fly larval burrowing prior to pupation). Melis et al. (2007) found increased pH and nitrate (NO3) concentrations in soils beneath one-yearold bison carcasses in a mixed conifer–oak forest in Poland, and increased Ca after three years. Melis et al. (2007) also reported that some bison carcasses had higher soil concentrations of K and phosphate (PO4) beneath the carcass compared to control soils. However, no differences in the plant community composition or plant heights, abundances, or diversity were associated with the carcasses (Melis et al. 2007).

In contrast, Towne (2000) found increased soil concentrations of inorganic N and P beneath large mammal carcasses in tallgrass prairie for up to three years postmortem, and recorded highly significant dynamics in plant species richness, diversity, and species-specific cover. Plant biomass initially decreased one year postmortem, but increased significantly two years postmortem before declining in subsequent years (Towne 2000). In the tundra of the Canadian Arctic, Danell et al. (2002) observed lush plant growth surrounding carcasses of muskoxen, and measured higher plant N concentrations within 1 m of the carcasses. Danell et al. (2002) also noted that herbivores avoided grazing the vegetation adjacent to the carcass, potentially contributing to the lush appearance of the plants. In an African scrub–savanna, Coe (1978) reported that soils beneath elephant carcasses exhibited leachate ‘‘crusts’’ of up to 40 cm deep and extending up to 2 m outward from the carcass. Soil N levels beneath the carcasses were elevated by three to eight times those of control soils; however, vegetative cover was considerably reduced in these areas, and was composed only of species characteristic of disturbed ground (Coe 1978). Finally, Vass et al. (1992, 2002) documented soil chemistry changes associated with decomposition of human cadavers, describing sub-cadaver soil increases in

volatile fatty acids, chloride, sulfate, sodium, ammonium, potassium, calcium, and magnesium.

## Comparisons of carrion vs. plant litter decomposition

The fundamental differences in the tissue characteristics and nutritional compositions between vertebrate carrion and plant litter lead to substantive differences in decomposition patterns. First, decomposition rates are obviously much faster for carrion than plant litter. Decomposition rate constants (on a daily basis) for plant biomass in different ecosystems range from 0.00048 in tropical forest to 0.00022 in deciduous forest, and to 0.00008 in xeric ecosystems (Harmon et al. 2001). Carrion decomposition coefficients are substantially larger, and in deserts, decomposition rates are up to three orders of magnitude faster in carrion than in plant litter.

With respect to substrate nutritional quality, plant litter decomposition rate is correlated with litter quality (N content and C:N ratios), such that litter higher in N and having lower C:N ratios decomposes more quickly than litter with low N concentration and high C:N ratios (Swift et al. 1979, Cadisch and Giller 1997). Carrion decomposition is consistent with this relationship, in that carrion’s N content of 6–12% (Table 1) is considerably higher than that of plant litter (typically 1–2% N). Carrion’s higher decomposition coefficients extend the correlation between k values and N content, although correlation with N-content and k1 values among vertebrate carcass types was not observed.

Patterns of change in chemical composition of the remaining decomposing substrates also differ between plant litter and carrion (Figs. 7–10). Plant litter tends to exhibit increases in N during decomposition (see example of Scots pine needle decomposition in Berg and Laskowski [2006:115]), whereas carrion shows continual N losses. Sulfur shows a similar reversed pattern of concentration change (increases in plant litter, decreases in carrion). Potassium in plant litter shows an initial decrease due to leaching, but then steadily increases in concentration, whereas in carrion, K concentrations quickly decline. Plant litter calcium content initially increases, and then decreases during decomposition; carrion calcium content continues to increase, particularly during the latter skeletal remains stage of carrion decomposition. Phosphorus content in plant litter tends to increase during decomposition, a pattern that also was observed in carrion.

Decomposition of wood materials (tree trunks, branches, and twigs) shows different rates based on bole diameter, although this pattern changes with moisture regimes. In drier ecosystems, desiccation of small-diameter wood pieces results in slower decomposition compared to larger-diameter wood boles that retain moisture (Erickson et al. 1985), whereas in more mesic environments, small-diameter boles decompose more quickly than larger branches due to having greater surface area to volume ratios (Foster and Lang 1982,

## Carrion contributions to nutrient cycling in the shrub–steppe ecosystem

At a landscape scale in our semiarid shrub–steppe ecosystem, vertebrate biomass comprises only a small percentage (0.06%) of the total available aboveground standing biomass (Table 6). Thus, quantitatively, carrion decomposition contributes minimally to the total ecosystem nutrient-cycling process. However, at the local patch-scale level, vertebrate carcasses can have a significant influence on soil nutrient status and turnover. Given the potentially high densities of some bird and small mammal species, many of which have short life spans, the overall role of carrion decomposition in cycling important limiting nutrients (e.g., N and P) may contribute substantially to the composite biogeochemical cycling of an ecosystem through generation of spatial heterogeneity and creation of islands of fertility. While the plant–soil effects observed from decomposing small-bodied animals may not be as obvious as those of larger species (e.g., the mule deer carcass shown in Appendix C), decomposition processes of small vertebrate species, which are vastly more abundant in most ecosystems, may prove equally significant for nutrient dynamics at the landscape scale,

because their cumulative effect is relatively more uniform in time and space.

Taken collectively, the results of our study and the work of previous researchers indicate clearly that the decomposition of vertebrate carrion varies markedly across ecosystems, among species, within microsites, and in different seasons. Scavenger impacts on carrion decomposition are site specific, and also vary by ecosystem, season, microhabitat, and carcass type and size. Carrion decomposition processes influence soil physical properties, microclimate, nutrient concentrations, and fauna, which in turn may alter, positively or negatively, the adjacent vegetation in terms of species composition, density, and productivity.

While this inherent variability in carrion decomposition may seem daunting, the basic principles involved in regulating the rates and outcomes of the vertebrate carcass can be applied to quantitatively predict the dynamics of a carcass’s fate. Carrion decomposition rate, at least in this shrub–steppe ecosystem, adheres to the temperature coefficient (Q10) of ;2, indicating a doubling of decomposition rate for every 108C rise in temperature. As a result, seasonal differences in mass loss rates can be predicted. Carrion decomposition in this semiarid ecosystem proceeds faster below ground than above ground. Wet-mass loss rates and amounts during the early phase of decomposition follow relationships with surface area to volume ratios of the carcass (but this may change in more mesic environments). Nutrient losses from carcasses occur in predictable sequences and influence sub-carcass soil chemistry and nearby adjacent vegetation assemblages. We caution, however, that current understanding of the environmental controls and rates of carrion decomposition and nutrient cycling processes are based on only a

small number of studies, utilizing a short list of vertebrate species, and occurring in only a few ecosystems. The nuances of carrion decomposition will undoubtedly provide many future opportunities to quantify and calibrate these principles across the world’s ecosystems, thereby developing a more complete understanding of carrion’s contribution to an ecosystem’s nutrient cycling processes.
